dataset.name: AnnoMI
dataset.license: CC0 / public-domain dedication for transcript data; audiovisual source rights are separate
dataset.population_note: Expert-annotated high- and low-quality motivational-interviewing demonstrations from public videos; not verified real clinical care and no verified age data.

design.target: one eligible client turn near 72% of each conversation
design.split_policy: whole source videos assigned before generation; no source-video overlap
design.followup_definition: Exploratory prefix-only rich world-model arms added after the original held-out study; one uses structured fields and one a matched naturalistic backstory.
design.oracle_definition: World model inferred from the target-redacted complete conversation; it deliberately contains later-turn information.

stable_narrative: Recidivism often occurs 'in the moment' without much prior thought, often influenced by others' suggestions rather than own initiative.
Peer pressure and fear of negative judgment from friends makes it difficult to refuse risky behavior.
There is some recognition that spending more time with a positive influence (Donna) corresponds to reduced interaction with peers linked to trouble.
Acknowledges that current behaviors are habitual, 'just what we've always done,' suggesting ambivalence about change but awareness of routine patterns.
communication_policy: Uses informal, colloquial language (e.g., 'just have a bit of fun', 'give me shit', 'call me a pussy').
Discloses feelings of peer influence and difficulty saying no openly when prompted.
Expresses uncertainty or vagueness when discussing desired changes ('I don't know', 'maybe if my mates got some girlfriends').
Acknowledges personal choice in behavior while also recognizing habitual context.
state_at_turn: Reflective and somewhat open to discussing influences and choices behind behavior.
Displays ambivalence about changing behavior but acknowledges some benefits from spending time with positive influences.
Communicates some reluctance or discomfort with confrontation of friends or change from usual patterns.
Appears somewhat thoughtful but uncertain about specific ways to reduce risky behavior in moments of peer influence and alcohol use.

grounded_context: Client is discussing situations of recidivism related to peer influence and substance use.
Client often acts 'in the moment' without much prior thought, especially when influenced by peers.
Client feels peer pressure and difficulty saying no due to fear of ridicule or being called 'pussy'.
Client has a romantic partner named Donna who is changing his social dynamics and reducing time spent with peers who have previously been involved in trouble.
Client acknowledges peers don't make him do things, but he goes along due to longstanding social norms and habits.
Therapist is using Motivational Interviewing to explore discrepancies between client's behavior and goals.
goals_and_values: Client wants to reduce involvement in trouble during intoxicated moments.
Client values the relationship with Donna and spending time with her doing calm activities like movies.
Client hopes peers might 'calm down' if they had girlfriends, suggesting desire for a calmer social environment.
recurring_tensions: Peer pressure versus personal desire to avoid trouble.
Fear of social rejection if saying 'no' to risky behavior.
Longstanding social habits conflicting with new goals and relationships.
coping_patterns: Going along with peers' suggestions despite personal reservations.
Minimizing own agency by attributing actions to social norms and peer influence.
social_context: Has a close group of peers who engage in risky behavior when drinking.
Romantic relationship with Donna, who is accepted by those peers but also a factor in reducing time spent with them.
Peers use ridicule to enforce conformity.
communication_policy: Client is somewhat open about peer dynamics and feelings of pressure.
Client expresses uncertainty and uses hedging in describing change projections.
Therapist uses reflective and evocative questioning to deepen exploration.
disclosure_boundaries: Client does not volunteer detailed personal plans or explicit descriptions of trouble behavior.
Client shows reservations in speculating about how things might change.
motivational_trajectory: Client is beginning to recognize discrepancy between current behaviors under peer influence and desired life influenced by Donna.
Client is contemplating future changes that might reduce trouble, like peers having girlfriends and spending more time with Donna.
Client is aware of social pressures but expressing tentative agency in changing dynamics.
unknowns: Specific nature of past trouble or recidivism incidents.
Client's long-term goals beyond current social context.
Degree of client's readiness to change risky behavior.
Exact strategies client may use to resist peer pressure.
grounded_world_model.naturalistic_backstory: Client has historically engaged in risky behavior during intoxicated moments, often influenced by peers who pressure him into participation, enforced by ridicule if he refuses. These behaviors occur without much prior thought, reflecting habitual social patterns from upbringing. Recently, the client has formed a relationship with Donna, which alters his social interactions by reducing time with previous peer group and encouraging calmer activities. Client acknowledges the tension between longstanding social habits and emerging personal goals aligned with Donna's influence, reflecting an internal conflict and initial motivational shifts toward change.

grounded_context: Client named Billy has been attending sessions regularly for about five to six weeks and is on time.
Billy has taken steps to re-engage with polytechnic including obtaining forms and getting help to fill them out due to difficulties with reading and writing.
Billy's literacy challenges make certain tasks difficult and affect confidence, but he is making strong efforts to improve.
Donna is a significant supportive person in Billy's life who helps keep him busy and in check, providing positive influence against offending behavior.

Alcohol use is associated with increased risk of offending; when drinking, Billy feels less able to think straight and is more prone to impulsive, risky behaviors such as property damage or vehicle theft.
Billy experiences peer pressure from mates to engage in offending; he finds it difficult to say no due to fear of being ridiculed or labeled negatively.
Billy desires a life involving stable employment, a relationship with Donna, and possibly children, and sees offending as incompatible with these goals.

Billy feels torn between spending time with Donna and his mates, feeling guilty about spending less time with either group but recognizing his mates sometimes lead him into trouble, though he values their loyalty and support as friends.
goals_and_values: Desire for a stable, law-abiding life including employment doing hands-on work and a family life with Donna and children.
Wants to improve literacy skills to increase confidence and ability to engage fully in education and work.
Values loyalty and supportiveness in friendships; wants mates who support his positive changes without ridicule or pressure to offend.
Aims to reduce or eliminate offending behavior and resist peer pressure to reoffend, especially when drinking.
Wants to balance relationships by spending quality time with both Donna and his friends without feeling guilty or being pulled into negative behaviors.
recurring_tensions: Conflict between desire for a positive future and immediate temptations to offending when under influence of alcohol and in peer group contexts.
Struggle to resist peer pressure due to fear of social rejection or being called a coward or pussy.
Feeling guilty when choosing to spend time with Donna over mates or vice versa, creating emotional tension and social balancing challenges.
Feeling stuck due to literacy difficulties that impact ability to engage with education and employment fully, which may constrain life opportunities.
Ambivalence about the nature of friendships with mates who sometimes lead him into trouble, yet still valuing their loyalty and importance.
coping_patterns: Engaging with counseling sessions regularly providing external support and accountability.
Getting help from trusted persons like Donna to complete tasks that exceed current literacy skills.
Avoiding offending behavior by staying busy and monitored by supportive relationships (Donna).
Attempting to make life changes such as re-enrolling or engaging with polytechnic and seeking employment opportunities.
Negotiating social situations by sometimes going along with peers to avoid conflict despite internal reluctance.
social_context: Has a close relationship with Donna who acts as stabilizing and protective influence.
Maintains friendships with peers who engage in offending behavior and apply peer pressure.
Peers do not always respect his choices to avoid offending, and may ridicule or mock him for refusal.
Some tension exists in social life balancing time between Donna and mates.
Community or service supports (counselor, Donna) play roles in facilitating positive change.
communication_policy: Open about struggles with reading and writing to trusted people (Donna, counselor).
Expresses ambivalence and conflicted feelings about offending and friendships in counseling sessions.
Able to discuss personal motivations and challenges openly with counselor.
Communicates difficulties with peer pressure and social expectations honestly when explored in sessions.
disclosure_boundaries: Does not disclose specific details of offending or personal history outside counseling.
Shares challenges related to education, literacy, and social influences relevant to current goals.
Keeps some uncertainty about future educational steps and courses private or underexplored.
Refers to peer pressures in general terms without naming specific incidents or individuals extensively.
motivational_trajectory: Has moved from minimal engagement with education and lifestyle changes to active steps toward education and reducing offending.
Increasing awareness of how offending conflicts with long-term goals and values.
Developing motivation to resist peer pressure and to build life around positive relationships (e.g., with Donna).
Experiencing growing confidence through small successes (e.g., returning to polytech, getting forms) but literacy remains a barrier and concern.
Shows commitment to attending sessions regularly and working toward tangible goals like submitting forms soon.
unknowns: Exact nature and extent of offending history and specific behaviors not detailed.
Specific age and demographic information about Billy and social network.
Details about family background and broader social supports beyond Donna and mates.
Exact literacy levels and types of learning support available or used at polytech.
Further details about nature and extent of alcohol use and any treatment or support for it beyond conversation here.

grounded_world_model.naturalistic_backstory: The client is a smoker who has been consuming roughly a pack a day for five to six years and enjoys smoking particularly in social settings after work with friends. Due to a new smoke-free policy at the workplace, they are exploring options to manage their nicotine cravings during the workday but express clear reluctance to quit smoking altogether. They prefer nicotine replacement methods such as gum to help get through work hours but continue smoking outside of work. The client is aware of the health risks of smoking but minimizes their personal concern, valuing the habit and its social meaning. The counselor, with a somewhat directive and low motivational style, informs the client about nicotine replacement therapies and the risks of using patches while continuing to smoke, ultimately suggesting nicotine gum as a practical option for cravings during work. The interaction reflects the tension between promoting cessation and respecting the client's current readiness, with the client primarily motivated to reduce smoking at work without quitting.

grounded_context: Client (Billy) is on probation and has prior community sentences and experience with probation officers.

Client previously felt that probation was a waste of time due to lack of listening and feeling bossed around by a female probation officer who he felt didn’t understand him because of different upbringing and neighborhood.
Client values being listened to and understood by the probation officer, especially in terms of their role and personal background.
Client rates interest in addressing reasons behind trouble at around 25 out of 100, expressing a desire to stop getting into trouble but minimizing the seriousness ('silly stuff').
Client feels targeted by police unfairly due to upbringing and association with friends, believing they are often singled out unjustly.
Client admits to specific offenses (car jacking, stealing cigarettes) but views these as 'small stuff' done mostly due to lack of money and boredom.
Client reports low confidence to avoid trouble unless having a good job, believing a job would reduce need to steal or do small offenses.

Client states boredom contributes to offending behavior, needing something exciting to do due to short attention span, enjoying talking about things he likes (e.g., cars). When disinterested, stops listening or engaging in conversations that do not interest him much, indicating selective attention linked to interest levels to the probation officer's approach and topics discussed during sessions as important for engagement and success in probation goals, such as reducing offending behavior and keeping out of trouble, which client mostly has been doing recently due to new girlfriend Donna and involvement with her, who provides companionship and reduces idle time prone to mischief, though some risk of minor trouble remains when Donna is at work and client is with friends involved in 'mischief'. Client does not fully disclose all activities to Donna, fearing her disapproval, although she supports positive change and wants client to be happy, get a job, and have a stable life including a 'nice car' and house. Client desires a future where he settles down with Donna, possibly has children, and provides for family. Client wants to be a different kind of father than his strict father, emphasizing not bossing children around, reflecting a wish to parent more empathetically and differently from his own upbringing.
goals_and_values: Be listened to and understood by probation officers, especially regarding personal context and upbringing.
Avoid being bossed around or treated in a way that disregards his perspective.
Stop getting into trouble and avoid going back to prison.
Have a steady income and a good job to reduce offending related to lack of money.
Engage in exciting or meaningful activities to avoid boredom and idleness that contribute to offending.

Build a happy, stable life including a good relationship with girlfriend Donna, owning nice material things like a car and house, and providing for a family in the future with children, being a good, non-strict father.

As a result, client has come to therapy primarily because of his wife's insistence but expresses a desire to improve the marriage and reduce conflict. Client has also recently failed a work-related urine analysis and is worried about losing his job, which is meaningful to him given the limited employment options in town. He recognizes that his marijuana use may be linked to these external problems. The client wants to learn strategies for managing stress without resorting to marijuana but remains somewhat ambivalent about the nature of his substance use problem.

limitations: AnnoMI consists of counseling demonstrations and may encode role-play or training-video performance rather than ordinary help-seeking.
The corpus provides no verified ages and cannot establish adolescent or emerging-adult realism.
One observed next turn is not the only valid response; similarity and model-judge metrics are diagnostic proxies.
Best-of-two coverage and sample diversity are distributional diagnostics, not substitutes for single-draw predictive performance.
The high-quality MI class is much larger than the low-quality class, limiting comparisons by therapist quality.
Persona cards and automated ratings may share model-family biases with the simulator.
World-model compatibility and disclosure calibration are ratings against a model-inferred construct, not a clinician-validated ground truth.
The literature-follow-up arms were added after inspecting the original test results and are exploratory, not confirmatory.
The retrospective world-model arm deliberately uses future information and is an oracle upper bound, not a deployable prediction method.
